title: How to manage cross-stitch project notes
subtitle: Keeping a record of materials, colours, and progress for each project
excerpt: Project notes record the details of a cross-stitch project so you can match materials if a skein runs out, resume the work after a break, and note what worked or did not work. A basic record includes the fabric count, the thread brand and colour numbers, the stitch count, the chart source, and a log of which areas have been completed.
sourceNotes: Project note-keeping practice for cross-stitch. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.
A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.

content.text: Project notes serve two functions: they let you replace materials mid-project without guessing at thread numbers, and they let you resume after a break without losing your place. At minimum, record the fabric count and brand, the
colour numbers and how many skeins were purchased, the chart source, and a note of which areas are complete.
Before starting, record the fabric details: brand,
count (14-count, 16-count, 18-count, etc.), and cut size. This lets you buy more of the same fabric if needed, or reference the same fabric for a repeat of the project.

Record each thread colour number alongside the quantity purchased. If you buy three skeins of a colour, note that. If you run out and need to return to the shop, you need the exact number, not an approximation of the shade.
Note the chart source: a book title and page number, a website and designer name, or a pattern PDF filename. If the chart is lost or damaged mid-project, the source note allows it to be recovered.

Keep a simple progress log: at the end of each session, mark on a printed chart copy which areas are complete, or write a short line in the notes such as 'completed upper left quadrant'. When you return to the project after a break, the log shows immediately where to resume.

Store the notes with the project: folded inside the project bag, clipped to the chart printout, or kept in the same box as the thread bobbins. Notes that are stored separately from the project are often lost before the project is finished.

items.symptom: The thread colour number on the paper band is worn off before you need to buy more
items.cause: The paper band wears quickly with handling and storage.
items.fix: Write the colour number on each bobbin directly with a permanent marker as soon as you wind the thread off the skein. The number on the bobbin is much more durable than the paper band.

items.symptom: You can't remember which area was done last or what row you were on
items.fix: Mark completed areas on a chart printout with a light coloured pencil as you finish each section. Even a simple X over a completed block is enough to orient yourself when you return to the project.

content.text: For a small first project, a single index card stored in the project bag is enough. For longer or more complex projects, a small notebook or a printed project sheet keeps everything organised. The habit of noting materials before starting pays off every time a project is picked up after a break.
